questions.q: Order a report's elements: body details, headline, lead (4W), byline, quote.
questions.a: headline → byline → lead → body details + quote. A wrong answer putting the quote in the lead shows pyramid misunderstanding — the lead is pure 4W.

questions.q: 'I was thrilled to see the amazing projects!!!' — fix for a report.
questions.a: 'The exhibition featured 40 student projects' — quantify and attribute instead of exclaiming. A wrong answer removing only exclamation marks keeps the first-person stance — the whole reporting posture must change.

questions.q: Where does 'said the Principal' attach, and why does the attribution matter?
questions.a: After the quoted clause — 'The standard was outstanding, said the Principal.' Attribution certifies the fact as reported, not invented — the mechanism that separates reports from opinions.

questions.q: An event report for the school magazine/newspaper: headline → byline → place+date line → lead answering What/When/Where/Who → body in inverted pyramid (details, quotes, outcome) → closing line on ______/verdict.

Fill in the blank: An event report for the school magazine/newspaper: headline → byline → place+date line → lead answering What/When/Where/Who → body in inverted pyramid (details, quotes, outcome) → closing line on ______/verdict.

Fill in the blank: The pyramid discipline: the lead alone must let a reader leave informed — 'The annual science ______ was held on 12 March in the main hall, drawing 40 projects from classes 9-12.' Middle paragraphs add a quote ('The innovation level was remarkable, said the Principal') and details; the tail carries what can be cut.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student produces a complete report with all format elements, inverted-pyramid body, integrated attributed quotes, and zero first-person narrative drift.
